questions.stem: Babur established the Mughal Empire after defeating whom in the First Battle of Panipat (1526)?
questions.explanation: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, the Sultan of Delhi, in the First Battle of Panipat on April 21, 1526, using artillery (gunpowder weapons) for the first time in Indian warfare, and established the Mughal Empire.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Taj Mahal in Agra was built by which Mughal emperor in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal?
questions.explanation: Shah Jahan (reigned 1628–1658) built the Taj Mahal between 1632 and 1653 as a mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Humayun lost the Mughal throne after being decisively defeated by Sher Shah Suri at the Battle of:
questions.explanation: At the Battle of Kanauj (also called the Battle of Bilgram) in May 1540, Sher Shah Suri routed Humayun, who had to flee India and live in exile for about 15 years before regaining the throne in 1555.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Which Mughal emperor introduced the syncretic religion Din-i-Ilahi in 1582?
questions.explanation: Akbar founded Din-i-Ilahi (Divine Faith) in 1582, an eclectic religious doctrine that drew elements from Islam, Hinduism, Zoroastrianism, and Christianity. It reflected his policy of sulh-i-kul (universal peace/tolerance).
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Battle of Haldighati (1576) was fought between Akbar's forces (led by Man Singh) and which Rajput ruler?
questions.explanation: The Battle of Haldighati (June 18, 1576) was fought between Akbar's general Man Singh I and Maharana Pratap of Mewar. Though Pratap had to retreat, he continued guerrilla resistance and was never fully subdued by Akbar.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The 'Dahsala' (ten-year settlement) revenue system under Akbar, fixing land revenue based on average prices and yields over ten years, was introduced by which finance minister?
questions.explanation: Raja Todar Mal, Akbar's brilliant finance minister, introduced the Dahsala or Ain-i-Dahsala system in 1580–82. It classified land and fixed revenue based on average production and prices over ten years — a landmark in Mughal revenue administration.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Ain-i-Akbari, a detailed administrative compendium covering the revenue system, military strength, and cultural life of Akbar's empire, was authored by:
questions.explanation: Abul Fazl (also written Abu'l-Fazl ibn Mubarak), Akbar's court historian and advisor, authored both the Akbarnama (biography of Akbar) and its third volume the Ain-i-Akbari (administrative record).
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Humayun-Nama, a biographical account of Emperor Humayun, was written by:
questions.explanation: Gulbadan Begum (Babur's daughter and Humayun's half-sister) wrote the Humayun-Nama at Akbar's request. It is one of the few historical works authored by a Mughal woman.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Mansabdari system under Akbar had two components that determined a noble's rank, pay, and military obligations. These two components were:
questions.explanation: The Mansabdari system was based on two numbers: Zat (personal rank, determining pay and status) and Sawar (number of cavalry a mansabdar had to maintain). For example, a mansab of 5000 zat / 5000 sawar was the highest below royalty.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Second Battle of Panipat (1556), which consolidated Mughal rule in India, was fought between Akbar's regent Bairam Khan and:
questions.explanation: The Second Battle of Panipat (November 5, 1556) was fought between Akbar's forces led by Bairam Khan and Hemu (also called Hemchandra), a Hindu general who had captured Delhi and Agra. Hemu was defeated and killed, restoring Mughal control.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Fatehpur Sikri, the magnificent city built by Akbar near Agra as his capital, was abandoned primarily because of:
options: It being sacked by Afghan invaders
Acute water scarcity making it unsustainable
A devastating fire that destroyed the palace
questions.explanation: Fatehpur Sikri (built 1571–85) was abandoned around 1585 primarily due to water scarcity. The city's water supply was insufficient to sustain a large population, and Akbar moved the capital to Lahore.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Aurangzeb reimposed the Jizya tax (abolished by Akbar in 1564) in which year?
questions.explanation: Aurangzeb reimposed the Jizya (poll tax on non-Muslims) in 1679. This was part of his reversal of Akbar's syncretic policies and his adoption of orthodox Sunni Islamic governance, which alienated many Hindu subjects.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The legendary Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Taus), encrusted with gems including the Koh-i-Noor diamond, was created during the reign of:
questions.explanation: The Peacock Throne was made during Shah Jahan's reign (around 1628–35). It was taken to Persia by Nadir Shah after his sack of Delhi in 1739. The Koh-i-Noor diamond was part of its decoration.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Which Mughal emperor wrote his own memoirs known as Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (Jahangirnama)?
questions.explanation: Emperor Jahangir (reigned 1605–1627) wrote the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (Jahangirnama), his personal memoirs in Persian. He was known for his love of art, nature, and justice, and his court produced some of the finest Mughal miniature paintings.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Babur's memoirs, considered one of the great autobiographies of world literature, are known as:
questions.explanation: Babur wrote his memoirs in Chaghatai Turkic; they are called the Baburnama (or Tuzuk-i-Baburi). They cover his life, campaigns, observations on nature and culture, and are a primary source for early 16th-century South/Central Asian history.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Empress Nur Jahan, who wielded enormous power in the Mughal court and even issued farmans and coins in her name, was the wife of which emperor?
questions.explanation: Nur Jahan (born Mehr-un-Nissa) was the 20th and most beloved wife of Emperor Jahangir. She was the de facto ruler for much of Jahangir's later reign and was the only Mughal empress to have coins struck in her name.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: After which Mughal emperor's death did the empire begin to disintegrate rapidly, with the Marathas, Rajputs, and regional powers asserting independence?
questions.explanation: Aurangzeb (died 1707) was the last powerful Mughal emperor. His long, costly Deccan campaigns drained the treasury, his religious intolerance alienated Hindu subjects, and his death unleashed a war of succession that shattered Mughal power.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Battle of Chausa (1539), one year before Humayun's final defeat, was also a victory for Sher Shah Suri. The battle was fought near which river?
questions.explanation: The Battle of Chausa (June 1539) was fought near Chausa on the bank of the Ganga in present-day Bihar. Sher Shah Suri trapped Humayun's army and inflicted a heavy defeat; Humayun barely escaped by swimming across the Ganga.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: In the Mughal system, a 'Jagir' was:
options: A hereditary land grant given permanently to nobles
A revenue assignment granted to mansabdars in lieu of cash salary
A type of land tax collected on agricultural produce
A military campaign launched against rebellious nobles
questions.explanation: A Jagir was a revenue assignment — the right to collect land revenue from a defined area — given to a mansabdar instead of cash pay. It was NOT hereditary; it was reassigned at the emperor's discretion, preventing the growth of a feudal landed aristocracy.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Bibi-ka-Maqbara in Aurangabad, often called the 'Poor Man's Taj', was built by which Mughal emperor in memory of his wife Dilras Banu Begum?
questions.explanation: Aurangzeb's son Azam Shah built Bibi-ka-Maqbara (1660s–70s) on Aurangzeb's orders for his wife Dilras Banu Begum (Rabia-ud-Daurani). Though built to rival the Taj Mahal, its lesser quality earned it the nickname 'Poor Man's Taj'.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Jahangiri Mahal in Agra Fort, despite its name, was actually built by which emperor?
questions.explanation: The Jahangiri Mahal inside Agra Fort was built by Akbar — the name is misleading. Akbar built the red-sandstone sections of Agra Fort; Shah Jahan later added the white marble structures. The palace was named after Jahangir posthumously.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Which art form flourished notably under Emperor Jahangir, known for naturalistic portrayals of animals, plants, and portraits?
options: Large-scale mural painting on mosque walls
questions.explanation: Mughal miniature painting reached its peak under Jahangir, who had a keen eye for art and nature. His court painters like Ustad Mansur (for nature studies) and Abul Hasan excelled in lifelike, naturalistic portraits and detailed studies of flora and fauna.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Akbar's policy of 'Sulh-i-Kul' (meaning 'absolute peace' or 'peace with all') was a guiding principle of his governance that promoted:
questions.explanation: Sulh-i-Kul was Akbar's doctrine of universal peace and tolerance. It meant treating all religions equally under state policy — a cornerstone of his administrative philosophy that included the abolition of the Jizya and promotion of inter-faith dialogue.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The famous Red Fort (Lal Qila) in Delhi, which served as the main residence of Mughal emperors for nearly 200 years, was built by:
questions.explanation: Shah Jahan built the Red Fort (Lal Qila) in Shahjahanabad (Old Delhi) between 1638 and 1648 when he shifted the Mughal capital from Agra to Delhi. The fort is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: In which year did Babur win the First Battle of Panipat, marking the formal beginning of the Mughal Empire in India?
questions.explanation: Babur won the First Battle of Panipat on April 21, 1526. He followed this with victories at the Battle of Khanwa against Rana Sanga (1527) and Battle of Ghaghra against Afghan chiefs (1529), consolidating Mughal rule.
questions.subject: History
